newsitem.title: INDIA: India, China hope to trim troops along border.
newsitem.headline: India, China hope to trim troops along border.

text.p: India and China hope to cut back troops along their disputed Himalayan frontier and spur trade and investment during a three-day visit by Chinese President Jiang Zemin from Thursday, Indian officials said.
Jiang will be the first Chinese president to visit India.

The world's two most populous nations, with one third of humanity between them, fought a brief border war in 1962. Troops are still deployed along both sides of a rugged line of control cutting across the towering Himalayan mountains.
The neighbours signed a path-breaking agreement in 1993 to ease tension along their 4,000 km (2,500 mile) border during a visit by former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao to Beijing.
In August 1995, India and China agreed to pull back their troops from four border posts in India's northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh, parts of which are claimed by China.
Indian officials said they expected further steps.

"We expect an agreement on confidence building measures in the military field along the line of actual control in the India-China border area," Salman Haider, the highest ranking civil servant in India's foreign ministry, said on Tuesday.
"The question of a mutually negotiated, mutually agreed reduction of forces as envisaged in the 1993 agreement is on the cards, is the next step," he told reporters.
Jiang will arrive in India after visiting the Philippines, where he attended the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum summit meeting. He is due to travel to Pakistan on Sunday.

The Chinese leader will be accompanied by Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, Minister of Foreign Trade Wu Yi, Civil Affairs Minister Doje Cering and Chairman of the Tibet Autonomus Regions Government Gyain Cain Norbu.
He will meet President Shankar Dayal Sharma, Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral.
Analysts said they did not expect any major breakthroughs.
"It is a goodwill visit and not a negotiating visit," political analyst B.G. Verghese said.
To keep relations on track, both sides were expected to avoid dwelling on two potentially contentious issues -- China's defence cooperation with India's arch-foe Pakistan, and Tibet.

Pakistan has enjoyed close relations with China, including defence cooperation, from the 1960s. In recent years, the two countries have been accused of secret nuclear and missile deals, which both have denied. India has been a reluctant critic.
"Nuclear is an important issue but it is not going to be the main issue," former foreign secretary J.N. Dixit said.
While Tibetan spiritual leader Dalai Lama's government-in- exile is based in northern India, India supports China's jurisdiction over Tibet.
Haider also predicted agreements on preventing crime and drug trafficking and on maintaining the consulate general of India in Hong Kong after the territory reverts to Chinese rule in 1997.
He said agreements on bilateral investment protection and strengthening of shipping services were being finalised.
In the 12 months ended March 31, 1995, two-way trade between China and India totalled a modest 31.7 billion rupees ($889 million).
China's exports to India were valued at 23.7 billion rupees, while India sold eight billion rupees' worth of goods to its northern neighbour.
India's exports to China include iron ore, fabrics, drugs and chemicals. Its imports from China include silk, raw coal, machinery and electronic goods.
